strengths: The paper identifies an important problem: commonly reported two-way identification scores can saturate and depend on the comparison pool, making them poor indicators of reconstruction quality.

The collection of 22 human ratings for each of 1,000 reconstruction pairs is potentially valuable, and the evaluation considers pairwise accuracy, Kendall correlation, and Pearson correlation rather than relying on a single statistic.

SEED combines complementary object-, caption-, and feature-based signals and achieves substantially higher agreement with the collected judgments than individual existing metrics (e.g., Pearson .817 versus .748 for EffNet).
The paper evaluates four recent decoding systems, analyzes semantic near-misses, examines failure cases of each SEED component, and includes some ablations.
The proposed loss is tested with three different decoding architectures, suggesting broad applicability, and its implementation is provided.
weaknesses: The central meta-evaluation appears to use the same 1,000 human-rated examples to select SEED's components, motivate their equal-weight combination, perform ablations, and report final performance. Without a held-out test set or cross-validation, the reported superiority may reflect metric selection overfitting and does not establish generalization.

All human judgments concern MindEye2 reconstructions from one dataset. Thus, the paper does not demonstrate that SEED's alignment with people generalizes to outputs from other decoding architectures, datasets, stimulus distributions, or failure modes, even though broad conclusions are drawn.

The human-study protocol is insufficiently documented: inter-rater agreement, annotator quality control, tie handling, aggregation, demographics, exclusion criteria, and statistical uncertainty are absent. The supplement also gives incomplete worker requirements and does not discuss consent or ethics oversight for the student evaluators.

The gain from the pairwise loss is very small for MindEye2 (SEED .474 to .475) and modest for the other models, with several existing metrics unchanged or worsened. Results are from apparently single runs without confidence intervals, significance tests, or seed variance, so the claim of significant and consistent improvement is unsupported.

The pairwise-loss implementation does not clearly match the mathematical definition: the paper specifies cosine similarities, whereas the supplied code uses unnormalized dot products unless normalization occurs elsewhere. Its temperature is undocumented in the experimental description, and the cubic N-by-N-by-N tensor creates a scalability concern that is not analyzed.

Object F1 is restricted to 82 mostly COCO categories, ignores multiplicity by default, and inherits detector errors. Cap-Sim inherits captioner and sentence-encoder biases. Equal averaging of three differently distributed scores is weakly justified, and behavior when no objects are detected is not clearly specified.

The metric contribution is technically simple—an unlearned average of existing detector, captioning, sentence-embedding, and EfficientNet outputs—and comparisons omit stronger contemporary learned image-similarity or vision-language evaluation models. This limits the novelty and leaves uncertainty about whether the gains are specific to the chosen candidate set.

Reproducibility is incomplete: the manuscript promises release of the judgments but provides no accessible artifact, and it lacks complete metric code, versions/checkpoints, preprocessing specifications, and enough details to reproduce all tables reliably.

strengths: The paper identifies a genuine evaluation problem: near-saturated identification scores can conceal semantically incorrect brain-decoding reconstructions.

Collecting 22 ratings for each of 1,000 image pairs is a useful effort. On these data, SEED improves over the strongest reported component, EffNet, from 78.0% to 81.0% pairwise accuracy, from 0.559 to 0.621 Kendall correlation, and from 0.748 to 0.817 Pearson correlation.
Object F1 and caption similarity are intuitive and comparatively interpretable, and the failure-case analysis helps explain why their combination with EffNet can be complementary.
The paper evaluates four existing decoding systems and tests the proposed training loss on three architectures. The loss implementation and several experimental details are provided.
weaknesses: The central meta-evaluation is not convincingly generalizable. All human ratings concern outputs from one model, MindEye2, on one NSD/MS-COCO test distribution. The same 1,000 pairs appear to be used to select components, choose their combination, and report SEED's final performance, with no held-out meta-evaluation set or cross-validation. The reported advantage may therefore reflect selection overfitting.

SEED is an uncalibrated equal-weight average of quantities with different definitions and ranges. No principled justification or held-out comparison against learned weights is given. The component search on the evaluation set further makes the incremental gain over EffNet difficult to interpret.

Object F1 is limited to 82 mostly COCO categories and discards counts, relations, attributes, and localization. Important edge cases, including images for which no GT or reconstruction category is detected and the precision/recall denominators become zero, are not defined. Consequently, the claim of a comprehensive semantic metric is too broad.

The human-study protocol is underreported. There is no inter-annotator agreement, uncertainty analysis, confidence interval, significance test, demographic information, attention-check procedure, or analysis separating MTurk workers from student evaluators. The paper also does not discuss consent or institutional review, and the stated payment of $0.03 per two-part judgment is not contextualized with completion time or effective hourly compensation.

The reported correlations treat 1,000 pairs as observations despite each score aggregating repeated ratings and despite possible dependence from shared images or subjects. Without bootstrap intervals or tests on paired differences, it is unclear whether SEED's modest improvement over EffNet is statistically reliable.

The evaluation lacks validation on independent reconstruction models and datasets with newly collected human judgments, as well as stress tests involving controlled semantic, attribute, count, spatial, and perceptual perturbations. Comparisons to stronger contemporary representation- and image-quality-based metrics are also limited.

Evidence for the pairwise hinge loss is weak relative to the claims of significant and consistent improvement. Some metrics decline, MindEye2's SEED change is only 0.474 to 0.475, and no multiple seeds, error bars, or statistical tests are reported. Qualitative examples are explicitly selected from cases where the loss improves SEED, introducing substantial selection bias.

The loss experiments modify the reproduced baselines, including reducing MindEye2's latent dimension and removing its low-level pipeline, so they do not cleanly establish gains for the published systems. In addition, the supplied code uses raw dot products while the mathematical definition uses cosine similarity; input normalization is not stated.

The pairwise ranking objective is presented as novel without adequate positioning against established pairwise, triplet, ordinal-ranking, and metric-learning losses. Its cubic batch computation and practical overhead are not analyzed.

Overall, the paper raises a worthwhile concern and offers a plausible metric, but the circular metric-selection protocol, narrow human-validation distribution, under-specified annotation study, and unconvincing loss experiments leave the principal claims insufficiently supported for a top-tier acceptance.

strengths: The paper identifies an important and underexamined problem: standard visual brain-decoding metrics can give near-perfect scores despite conspicuous semantic errors. The motivation is clear and supported by intuitive examples. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/experiments/runs/20260921_han_gpt_all_anonymized_review/scratch/6fd49387934b4880b53366336f533f1a/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

The collection of 22 ratings for each of 1,000 image pairs is potentially valuable. On these data, SEED substantially outperforms established metrics, reaching 81.0% pairwise accuracy, 0.621 Kendall correlation, and 0.817 Pearson correlation.

Combining object presence, caption semantics, and visual features is sensible, interpretable, and empirically complementary. The component analysis and failure examples help explain why the combination improves over each constituent.

Re-evaluating four recent decoding systems exposes the practically relevant semantic near-miss phenomenon, while testing the proposed loss on three architectures provides broader evidence than a single-model experiment.
weaknesses: The central meta-evaluation lacks a held-out test set or cross-validation. SEED's components and equal-weight combination appear to have been selected using the same 1,000 human-rated pairs on which its headline correlations are reported. This creates substantial selection bias. Moreover, all human-rated reconstructions come from MindEye2 and NSD, so generalization to other decoders, datasets, and image distributions is unverified.

The comparison set omits several strong contemporary perceptual and semantic metrics, such as DINO/DINOv2 features, LPIPS, DreamSim, CLIPScore, and stronger vision-language-model evaluators. Consequently, the claim that SEED provides the most accurate semantic evaluation is not yet established against the strongest plausible alternatives.

No confidence intervals, bootstrap analysis, or significance tests are reported for differences among correlated metrics. The human-study description also omits inter-rater reliability, rating aggregation details, annotator-level quality control, demographic information, and ethics or consent procedures, including how the additional student evaluators were recruited.

Object F1 is restricted to 82 predefined COCO-derived categories, ignores multiplicity, relationships, and attributes, and appears undefined when no objects are detected in one or both images unless an unstated convention is used. Averaging it directly with two cosine/correlation scores having potentially different ranges and calibration is insufficiently justified.

The pairwise-loss evidence is overstated. Gains are small for MindEye2 and UniBrain, several existing metrics degrade, no multiple-seed variation or significance analysis is provided, and the qualitative examples are explicitly selected from cases benefiting most from the loss. The final selected hyperparameters are also not reported.

The published loss implementation uses temperature-scaled dot products, whereas the mathematical definition uses cosine similarities; equivalence depends on normalization that is not stated. Together with modified baseline architectures, missing chosen hyperparameters, and promised rather than presently available data/code, this limits reproducibility.

strengths: Addresses an important evaluation problem: commonly reported identification metrics can saturate while reconstructed images still contain substantial semantic errors.
Proposes an interpretable composite metric combining object presence, caption semantics, and global visual features; the component analysis supports their complementarity.
The primary human study is relatively substantial, with 1,000 image pairs, 22 ratings per pair, and high reported inter-rater agreement.
SEED improves over all evaluated baselines on pairwise accuracy, Kendall correlation, and Pearson correlation, with reported confidence intervals against the strongest baseline.
Includes useful robustness checks across off-the-shelf component models, a second dataset/decoder setting, qualitative failure analysis, and evaluation of five decoding models.
The manuscript is generally clear, and its metric definitions, object vocabulary, survey interface, and several ablations are documented.
weaknesses: The principal methodological concern is evaluation leakage: SEED's components and their combination are selected based on the same 1,000-pair human dataset used to report its main performance. There is no held-out validation/test split or cross-validation, so the claimed gain may partly reflect metric selection on the test set.

The generalization evidence is limited. The only independent setting contains just 50 images and 10 student raters, uses a different dataset-specific object vocabulary, and yields only a small improvement over EffNet. This is insufficient to establish broad robustness across datasets, subjects, reconstruction distributions, and laboratories.

Statistical significance is assessed by bootstrapping only evaluators, despite the claims concerning generalization over images. A hierarchical bootstrap over both images and raters, with the full metric-selection procedure nested inside resampling, would be more appropriate.

The baseline set omits several relevant modern perceptual or human-aligned image-similarity approaches, such as LPIPS, DINO-family features, and learned perceptual-similarity metrics. Consequently, superiority over the strongest applicable alternatives is not established.

The equal-weight average is insufficiently justified. Its components have different ranges and distributions, and no held-out comparison against normalization, weight tuning, or alternative aggregation is given.

Object F1 depends on a manually chosen closed vocabulary that changes between NSD and GOD, ignores counts and relations, and does not define important edge cases such as images with no detected ground-truth or reconstructed objects. These choices limit metric portability.

There are reporting inconsistencies: Cap-Sim's Pearson correlation is .666 in Table 1 but .683 in Table 5, while Table 6 marks EffNet and SwAV as lower-is-better even though the text defines correlation-based, higher-is-better versions. These discrepancies weaken reproducibility.

The human-study documentation lacks key details such as annotator demographics, consent or ethics review, quality-control procedures beyond the MTurk Masters filter, exclusions, and the exact pairwise-accuracy construction. The very low payment of $0.03 for two judgments also warrants justification.

The neuroscience motivation is largely post hoc: the proposed components do not operationally model the claimed stages of human visual attention, so this framing should be presented as intuition rather than neuroscientific grounding.

Claims such as achieving the highest human alignment and generalizing well are stronger than supported by the current experimental design. Overall, the work is promising and technically plausible, but the missing held-out evaluation and incomplete statistical validation place it slightly below the top-tier acceptance threshold.

strengths: The paper identifies an important evaluation problem: near-saturated identification scores can obscure meaningful semantic errors in brain-decoded images.
The primary human study is reasonably substantial, with 22 ratings for each of 1,000 MindEye2 reconstruction pairs and reported high inter-rater agreement.
Object F1 and Cap-Sim are intuitive and interpretable, and the paper includes component combinations, alternative model choices, qualitative failure cases, and a small cross-dataset validation.

SEED shows consistently higher correlation with the collected human judgments than the conventional metrics considered, while the re-evaluation of five decoding systems illustrates potential practical utility.
weaknesses: The principal meta-evaluation is not held out from metric development. The same MindEye2/NSD human judgments appear to motivate the components, select design choices, compare combinations, and establish the final equal-weight ensemble. Without a predefined split, cross-validation, or a genuinely independent large test set, the reported advantage is vulnerable to selection overfitting.

The only independent validation contains just 50 Mind-Vis/GOD images and 10 student raters. Object F1 is also adapted using the GOD test-class list. This is insufficient evidence for broad generalization across image distributions, reconstruction artifacts, subjects, and decoding methods.

The baseline set is too narrow for a paper proposing a general semantic image-similarity metric. It emphasizes metrics historically used in brain decoding but omits stronger modern perceptual and human-aligned representation metrics. Consequently, the claim that SEED is the most human-aligned alternative is not established against the relevant broader literature.

The statistical analysis bootstraps only evaluators, apparently treating the 1,000 images as fixed. It therefore does not capture image-sampling uncertainty or metric-selection uncertainty. Significance is reported only for the primary development dataset, while claims about robustness rely on the much smaller secondary experiment.

SEED is a heuristic uncalibrated average of three quantities with different ranges and statistical meanings. Equal weighting is not justified independently, and the method can inherit correlated biases from an object detector, captioner, sentence encoder, and ImageNet classifier.

Object F1 has substantial coverage and construct-validity limitations: it uses a manually chosen set of 82 categories, merges category existence while ignoring counts and relations, includes overlapping labels such as person/man/woman, and depends on detector confidence calibration. Changing the category vocabulary for GOD further limits comparability across datasets.

Cap-Sim compresses each image into a single generated caption, so omitted objects or hallucinated attributes can dominate the score. The paper provides examples of this problem but no systematic analysis across captioning models, demographic attributes, or adversarial/out-of-distribution reconstructions.

Several secondary findings are weakly supported. The semantic-near-miss taxonomy and denominator are not adequately specified, the 0.3 detector threshold and semantic-detail-miss cutoffs are arbitrary, and neither failure-mode statistic is validated against human labels or accompanied by uncertainty estimates.

There are reporting and reproducibility concerns. Cap-Sim's Pearson correlation is 0.666 in Table 1 but 0.683 in Table 5; Figure 3 does not expose results for each component combination; exact checkpoints, preprocessing, feature layers, pairwise-accuracy construction, and annotation quality-control procedures are underspecified. Reporting p=0 is also statistically inappropriate.

The novelty is limited: SEED is primarily an average of object-set overlap, caption-embedding similarity, and an existing EfficientNet similarity score. The proposed connection to two-stage human visual attention is largely motivational and does not substantively derive or validate the metric design.

The human-evaluation protocol lacks important details such as attention checks, rejection criteria, randomization, annotator demographics, timing or compensation analysis, and ethics/consent oversight. These omissions matter because human ratings are the central ground truth.

Overall, the work highlights a genuine problem and contains promising empirical observations, but the lack of held-out metric validation, incomplete baseline coverage, heuristic construction, and insufficiently supported generalization claims prevent it from meeting the evidentiary standard of a top-tier acceptance.

strengths: The paper identifies an important and timely evaluation problem: near-saturated identification scores can obscure substantial semantic errors in visual brain reconstructions.

SEED is intuitive and interpretable, combining complementary object-, caption-, and feature-level signals. The component analyses and qualitative failure cases help explain why the combination can outperform individual metrics.
The primary human study is substantial, covering 1,000 image pairs with 22 ratings per pair, and reports high aggregate inter-rater reliability.

The empirical gains are meaningful: SEED improves over the strongest existing baseline, EffNet, across pairwise accuracy, Kendall correlation, and Pearson correlation. The paper also provides confidence intervals for these improvements.

The authors include several useful robustness and ablation studies, including alternative grounding, captioning, and text-encoding models; all component combinations; VQA-based alternatives; and a second dataset/model setting.
Re-evaluating five existing decoding systems demonstrates practical relevance and reveals interpretable failure modes that conventional near-saturated metrics conceal.
The manuscript is clear, well organized, and unusually candid about cases where SEED and its individual components fail.
weaknesses: The principal methodological concern is evaluation-set reuse. The components and their equal-weight combination appear to have been selected by examining alignment on the same 1,000 human-rated examples used for the headline results. Figure 8 explicitly searches metric combinations on this set. Without a development/test split or validation on a comparably sized independent benchmark, the reported advantage may be optimistically biased.

The only independent validation contains just 50 examples and 10 student evaluators. Moreover, Object F1 is changed from a fixed 82-category COCO vocabulary to the GOD dataset's 50 class names. This dataset-specific customization weakens the claim that a fixed SEED metric generalizes across datasets.

The baseline suite is dominated by metrics historically used in brain decoding. Stronger contemporary general-purpose similarity baselines—such as DINO-family features, LPIPS/DreamSim-style learned perceptual metrics, newer vision-language encoders, or capable VLM judges—are absent. Thus, the evidence supports improvement over current field practice more strongly than broad state-of-the-art semantic evaluation.

The equal weighting of Object F1, Cap-Sim, and EffNet is insufficiently justified. Their ranges and score distributions differ, and no held-out comparison against normalization, learned weights, or simple regression is provided.

Statistical uncertainty is estimated by bootstrapping only over evaluators, treating the 1,000 images as fixed. Resampling both images and evaluators would better support population-level generalization and could yield wider intervals. Reporting ICC(2,n), rather than also ICC for individual raters, can additionally make agreement appear stronger because it measures reliability of the aggregate.

Object F1 is tied to a restricted category vocabulary, ignores counts by default, and has underspecified edge cases when no objects are detected. Both the detector and captioner may also benefit from COCO-related pretraining on the NSD natural-scene domain, so broader out-of-domain validation is needed.

There is at least one numerical inconsistency: Cap-Sim's Pearson correlation is 0.666 in Table 1 but 0.683 in Table 5. Reproducibility is also not fully assessable from the manuscript because the stated code/data location is absent and the human data are described partly as a future release.

The human-study documentation lacks timing, quality-control/attention-check details, demographics, consent or ethics information, and justification that $0.03 for two judgments per image pair constitutes appropriate compensation. These omissions should be addressed, even if no formal ethics approval was required.

Overall, the work is promising and potentially useful, but the absence of a substantial untouched test set and stronger modern baselines leaves the central superiority claim just short of the evidence expected for acceptance at a top-tier venue.
